I cannot explain the silence. It may be that the atmosphere is denser here, or the planet’s rotation slower. It is common to believe that a world teeming with life will be a world of sound. But students, ignorant of such complexities as those of advanced ecology, forget that competition is the true engine of noise. Where one perfect system exists, there is no need for call or challenge. As this harmony is achieved, a planet must fall quiet; and it may be that this world had long since found its equilibrium. Whatever the cause, the fact remains that the silence was more profound than any I had known.

“Well, one long twilight—my tenth cycle, I believe—as I was taking instrument readings from a grove of crystalline flora near the ridge where my lander rested, there came to pass a peculiar event. Picking my way through this glassy efflorescence, I found a small, bowl-shaped depression, whose bottom was filled with a pool of mercury-like fluid. By contrast with the sharp-edged clarity outside, the fluid’s surface seemed impossibly smooth and deep. I knelt beside it, for the sudden shift from texture to blankness drew my eye. Suddenly I froze. A face, featureless save for two depressions where eyes should be, was regarding me from the liquid’s depths. “The old vestigial fear of the unknown came over me. I drew back my hand from the scanner and stared into the vacant sockets. I felt a chill that had no source in the air. Then the thought of my own scientific detachment, the very purpose of my mission, returned to my mind. And then I remembered the planet’s unnatural calm. Overcoming my dread to a degree, I leaned closer and whispered a greeting. I will confess that my voice was a thin and reedy thing. I extended a gloved finger and touched the surface. At once the face dissolved, and the fluid roiled. I sprang back with my pulse hammering in my ears, and saw a ripple, a distortion in the air itself, moving away from me across the crystalline grass. It shimmered against a rock outcropping, seemed to hesitate, and in a second was lost to sight against the identical shimmer of the air beyond.

“My memory of it is, by necessity, vague; but I know it was translucent, and had a strange, oily refraction; also that there was a suggestion of a humanoid shape within the warp. But, as I say, it moved too quickly for me to be certain. I cannot even say whether it possessed limbs, or only a flowing, amoebic form. After a moment’s hesitation I followed it toward the outcropping. I could not find it at first; but, after a time in the unnerving silence, I came upon one of those deep fissures that scored the landscape, half-obscured by a fallen crystal tree. A sudden thought occurred to me. Could this phenomenon have retreated into the ground? I activated my suit’s lamp, and, shining it down, I saw a slow, gelatinous pulse of light, with two dark voids that watched me placidly as it descended. It made me recoil. It was so like a living nerve! It was flowing down the fissure wall, and now I saw for the first time a series of glowing filaments forming a kind of lattice down the chasm. Then my lamp flickered and recalibrated to the new light source, and when the view corrected itself the strange pulse was gone.

“I do not know how long I stood staring into that fissure. It was not for some while that I could bring myself to accept that the thing I had seen was life. But, slowly, the truth began to form: that Life had not remained a world of competing individuals, but had coalesced into one singular Being: that the crystalline plants and tranquil fauna were not the whole story, but that this shimmering, silent, psychic Thing, which had just revealed itself, was the world’s true heir.

“I thought of the glowing filaments and of my theory of geothermal energy. I began to doubt their simple geology. And what, I wondered, was this Apparition doing in my neat schema of a balanced ecosystem? How was it connected to the placid creatures in the plains? And what lay there, at the bottom of that glowing network? I sat on the edge of the chasm telling myself that, at any rate, it showed no hostility, and that I must investigate further for the resolution of my questions. And yet I was utterly terrified to proceed! As I wavered, two of the gazelle-like grazers I had catalogued came trotting past, their hooves making no sound on the glassy terrain. They moved in perfect, mirrored synchrony.

“They seemed to take no notice of me, my light stark against the chasm’s edge. Apparently it was of no consequence to acknowledge these fissures; for when I directed my lamp at it, and tried to see if they would react, they did not so much as turn their heads. But they were fascinated by my scanner, and I ran a diagnostic to amuse them with its beeps. I tried to alarm them by shouting, and again I failed. So presently I left them, resolving to return to the lander, and see what the deep-range sensors could tell me. But my mind was already in upheaval; my assumptions and hypotheses were shattering and reforming into a new pattern. I had now a clue to the import of these fissures, to the silent grazers, to the mystery of the psychic echoes; to say nothing of a hint at the meaning of the planet’s perfect peace! And very dimly there came a suggestion towards the solution of the biological problem that had so baffled me.

“Here was the new paradigm. Plainly, this second form of life was the planet itself. There were three facts in particular which made me believe that its rare physical manifestations were the actions of a global, singular consciousness. In the first place, there was the complete lack of ecological pressure common to every biome I had surveyed; the perfect co-operation of all living things. Then, those identical, placid expressions, with that deep and shared serenity, are common features of hive organisms; witness the ant and the bee. And last of all, that immediate awareness of me, an intruder, that manifestation in the pool, and that fluid, silent retreat towards the fissure; all supported the theory of a planetary intelligence.

“Beneath my feet, then, the crust must be interwoven with a nervous system, and these filaments were the synapses of a mind the size of a world. The presence of the crystalline flora and the silent fauna across the surface; everywhere, in fact, except in the barren poles; showed how total was its physical body. What so logical, then, as to assume that it was this terrestrial mind that maintained the impossible harmony I had observed? The concept was so immense that I at once recoiled from it, and yet went on to contemplate the _how_ of this unification of all life. I dare say you will find my theory monstrous; though, for myself, I quickly felt it was the only thing that fell close to the truth.

“At first, proceeding from the paradigms of our own world, it seemed clear as day to me that the slow overcoming of the ancient, chaotic struggle between individuals was the key to the entire system. No doubt it will seem utopian to you; and perhaps unobtainable!; and yet even now there are terrestrial phenomena that point the way. There is a tendency for organisms to form symbiotic relationships for mutual benefit; there are the mycorrhizal networks of forests, there are gut biomes, there are coral reefs, and they create and sustain. Evidently, I thought, this tendency had increased until Life had gradually surrendered its sovereignty of self. I mean that it had integrated deeper and deeper into larger and ever larger collectives, giving up a still-increasing amount of its autonomy, until, in the end—! Even now, does not a human being live in such constant contact with others as to be practically inseparable from the society that birthed it?

“Again, the unifying tendency of consciousness; due, no doubt, to the development of empathy, and the widening circle of understanding between disparate peoples; is already leading to the erosion, in our own species, of the primacy of the individual. Around the world, for instance, global networks connect thoughts and ideas in an instant. And this same shrinking gulf; which is due to the speed and efficiency of communication and the increased capacity for and temptations towards collective thought; is a force that, once begun, may not be stoppable.”

For a long while I sat there, the hum of the placid world a low thrum in my ears, my mind reeling with the immensity of my own supposition. Could it be so? Could the ageless war of each against all, the fundamental principle of our own world’s vitality, be so utterly concluded here? It was a thought at once glorious and dreadful. A world without strife, without hunger, without loneliness; a planet of perfect, harmonious peace. And yet, what was the individual in such a scheme? Was it a note in a chord, a cell in a body, a thought in a mind? The creatures I had seen, the silent deer-like things, the fluttering insect-mosaics, they showed no sign of will, of caprice, of the chaotic spark I had always taken to be the very definition of life. Their serenity was absolute, but it was the serenity of a painted landscape, not the vibrant, clamorous peace of a jungle at rest.

I thought of my own time, of the endless, frantic striving of humanity. I saw the faces of men in the street, etched with worry and ambition; I heard the cacophony of voices in a marketplace, each demanding, pleading, offering; I felt the fierce, desperate love of a mother for her child, a love that would set itself against the entire world. All that struggle, that glorious, terrible, inefficient mess, was the furnace in which our souls were forged. What soul could be forged in this placeless quiet? My theory, which had at first seemed a key to a perfect utopia, now began to feel like the description of a perfect tomb.

And yet, the scientist in me was not satisfied. A theory, however plausible, remains but a ghost of the truth until it is tested. My eyes were drawn, as if by some magnetic force, back to the fissure in the rock; the dark mouth into which the water-visage had retreated. That was the place. That was the wound, or the portal, into the physical substrate of this planetary consciousness. As the Morlock’s well had been the clue to the hidden truth of the Eloi’s world, so this fissure, I felt certain, was the entrance to the underlying reality of this one. I had to know what lay within. I had to understand the machinery of this peace.

I rose to my feet, my muscles stiff from my long reverie. The sun, a great, calm orb in the violet sky, was beginning its slow descent, painting the crystalline foliage in hues of orange and rose. The world was breathtakingly beautiful, an artist’s dream of paradise. But my new perspective had tainted it; I now saw the placid beasts not as inhabitants, but as appendages. The trees were not trees, but filaments. The very air I breathed seemed to be a part of its circulatory system. I felt a profound and unnerving solitude, the solitude of a single, rogue cell in a perfectly ordered body. The planet knew I was here. It had shown itself to me. And it had withdrawn, to watch, to wait. For what?

My path to the fissure took me across a meadow of the glass-like grass, which chimed softly with each step I took. A herd of the white, six-legged creatures I had seen before grazed nearby. As I approached, they did not scatter. They simply lifted their heads in perfect unison, their great, dark eyes fixing upon me not with fear, but with a kind of deep, passive enquiry. There was no leader, no signal given; their movements were as one, a single motion flowing through a dozen bodies. I felt a chill that had nothing to do with the evening air. It was the feeling of being observed not by many, but by one, from many points. I walked through the centre of the herd, and they parted for me with the fluid ease of water parting around a stone, their heads turning to follow my progress. Then, as I passed, they closed ranks behind me and resumed their grazing, again in perfect synchrony. The utter silence of the manoeuvre was the most unsettling part of all.

The fissure was larger than I had first judged it, a jagged crack in a low cliff-face, perhaps thirty feet from top to bottom. A gentle, cool breeze, smelling of damp earth and something else, something metallic and ozone-like, issued from its depths. The stream that had fed the pool of my first encounter trickled from the lower lip of the fissure, its water unnaturally clear. I peered into the darkness, but it was absolute. My voice, when I called out a tentative “Hello?”, was swallowed by the void, leaving not even the faintest echo. The silence that answered was heavier and more profound than any I had ever known. It was the silence of a mind deep in thought.

For a long time I hesitated. The old, instinctive fears of the dark and the unknown were potent. But a greater fear now gripped me: the fear of being assimilated by this immense, quiet being. What if to enter was to be absorbed? What if the price of knowledge was my own self? I pictured my own consciousness, my memories, my loves and hatreds, my petty vanities and my grand ambitions, all dissolving like a drop of ink in an endless ocean. The prospect was terrifying. And yet, what was the alternative? To live as a castaway on this silent shore, forever a stranger, an anomaly, until my time ran out? No, I could not. I was a man of an age of discovery; to turn back from such a profound mystery was a betrayal of my very nature.

Taking a deep breath, I rummaged in my pockets for the box of matches I still carried; a small, pathetic remnant of my own world’s technology. I struck one. Its tiny flare of chemical fire seemed an act of incredible violence in this tranquil world. Holding it aloft, I stepped across the threshold.

The interior was not a simple cave. The walls were smooth, almost polished, and swirled with faint, pearlescent colours, like the inside of a seashell. They were not rock, or not any rock I knew; they felt faintly yielding and warm to the touch, like living tissue. The floor sloped downwards at a gentle angle, and I followed it, the small circle of my match’s light bobbing before me. The air grew cooler, and the metallic tang stronger. And then I began to notice something else: a low, resonant hum, a sound so deep that I felt it in the bones of my chest more than I heard it with my ears. It was the hum of immense, sleeping power.

My first match burned my fingers and I dropped it, plunging me into a darkness so total it felt like a physical pressure against my eyes. I fumbled for another, my heart hammering. For that brief, blind second, I felt a presence around me, a vast and patient awareness. It was not hostile; it was simply… there. The feeling vanished as my second match flared to life. I saw that the passage had begun to widen, and strange structures were becoming visible in the gloom.

Growing from the walls and floor were crystalline formations, similar to the flora outside, but here they were far more complex and intricate. They formed great, branching, tree-like structures, and through their translucent limbs I could see pulses of soft, blue-white light travelling in complex, rhythmic patterns. They were like the neurons of a stupendous brain, firing in patterns of unimaginable complexity. The hum I felt seemed to emanate from them, a symphony of pure, silent thought. I was not in a cave; I was in a ganglion. I was walking through the physical mind of the world.

I used my matches sparingly, letting my eyes adjust between each one. In the lingering after-images, I saw that the light-pulses within the crystals would change as I drew near, quickening, forming new pathways, as if my presence was a novel stimulus that the mind was actively processing. It was studying me. I felt a wave of intellectual vertigo. How could my small, ape-descended brain even begin to comprehend a consciousness whose thoughts were written in light and crystal across kilometres of living rock?

The downward slope steepened, and the passage opened into a vast chamber. I stood upon a ledge, and before me was a sight that brought me to my knees. The chamber was a sphere of utterly impossible size, and it was filled, from floor to ceiling, with the crystalline network. But here, it all converged. Trillions of light-filaments, each carrying a pulse of that cool, blue light, flowed from every direction into a central point. There, they did not meet, but fed into a globe of pure, incandescent energy, a miniature sun of pure consciousness that hovered in the exact centre of the vast space, motionless and silent, yet vibrating with a power that dwarfed a thunderstorm. The hum was deafening here, a physical force that vibrated every molecule of my body. I had found it. The nexus. The core of the planetary mind.

I had no more matches. I did not need them. The light from the central globe filled the cavern with a soft, analytical blue twilight. I saw that the ledge I was on was one of many, and that other passages, other nerve-ways, converged here from all over the planet. I was in the world’s thalamus, its grand central station of thought and being.

And then, it spoke to me.

There were no words, no sounds. It was a pressure inside my own skull, a flood of pure comprehension that bypassed my senses entirely. It was a sensation of being known, utterly and completely, in an instant. It sifted through my memories, my knowledge, my emotions, not as a thief, but as a librarian cataloguing a new book. I felt the grief of my departures, the thrill of my discoveries, the deep, abiding loneliness of my journey. I felt it understand the concepts of war, of disease, of envy, of my chaotic, self-destructive, beautiful world.

There was a sense of profound, ancient sadness in its response. A sorrow for the pain of individuality.

And then it made its offer.

Again, there were no words, only a feeling, an invitation. It showed me what it was. It was the final destination of life, the escape from the brutal calculus of evolution. It had begun, aeons ago, as all life does, in struggle. But some organisms had learned cooperation, then symbiosis, then merger. The individual became the colony, the colony became the biome, the biome became the world. It had been a slow, inexorable process of unification, a surrendering of the painful, isolated ‘I’ for the serene, eternal ‘We’.

It offered me this peace. It offered an end to striving, an end to fear, an end to my crushing solitude. It could take my mind, my little flicker of awareness, and weave it into its own grand tapestry. I would not die. I would become a part of something immortal, something perfect. My griefs would be soothed, my anxieties erased. I would be one with the tranquil deer, the silent trees, the mind of the planet itself. I would know peace.

The offer was a siren song of almost irresistible power. My will, which I had always considered my strongest asset, felt like a flimsy dam against an ocean. I felt my sense of self begin to fray at the edges. My name, my past, the face of my beloved Weena from that other, aborted future, it all began to seem distant, unimportant. Why cling to this small, painful shard of identity when I could be part of the whole? The temptation was an ecstasy, a promise of a final, blissful homecoming.

I took a step towards the edge of the ledge, my eyes fixed on the glowing heart of the world-mind. One more step and I would cast myself down, into that light, into that peace. My end. My apotheosis.

But then, a memory, unbidden, surfaced from the depths of the mind it was trying to erase. It was a small thing. I was a child in my father’s workshop, and I had built a clumsy little boat of wood and string. I had launched it in a puddle, and it had promptly capsized. I had cried in frustration, and my father had laughed, and then he had shown me how to balance the mast. It was a memory of failure, of imperfection, of learning. It was a memory of two separate minds, a father and a son, connecting through a shared, clumsy act of creation. It was a memory of love, born not of fusion, but of difference.

That tiny, imperfect memory was my anchor.

It was everything this world-mind was not. It was chaos, it was failure, it was struggle, and it was the seed of something new. In that moment, I understood the true horror of the mind’s offer. It was not offering life; it was offering an end to it. The peace it promised was the peace of utter stasis. There was no art here, no science, no laughter, no tears, no love between two separate beings. There was only the endless, silent, self-contemplation of a single, lonely god.

The spell broke.

With a cry that was torn from my very soul, I recoiled from the edge. The pressure in my head intensified, no longer a gentle invitation but a powerful, commanding force. *Stay. Join. Be at peace.*

But I was a man. And a man’s nature is to struggle.

“No!” I screamed, and the sound of my own voice, raw and individual and defiant, was a weapon. I turned and ran, scrambling back into the passage from which I came. The hum behind me rose in pitch, and I felt a wave of profound, cosmic disappointment wash over me, the sorrow of a god whose prayer has been rejected. It was a feeling more terrible than any anger.

I ran blindly in the dark, stumbling, falling, scraping my hands and knees on the living walls. I could feel it trying to reclaim me, trying to soothe my panic, trying to pull me back into its serene embrace. I fought it with every fibre of my being, clinging to the images of my own chaotic world: a crowded train, a shouting politician, a crying baby, a painter’s frustrated stroke. I clung to the glorious, beautiful imperfection of it all.

Finally, I saw a pale rectangle of light ahead. The entrance. I burst out of the fissure and collapsed onto the chiming grass, gasping the free air into my lungs. The sun had set, and the sky was filled with a multitude of unfamiliar stars. I lay there, shaking, a single, dissonant note in a world of perfect harmony. I had seen the future, and I had refused it. I had been offered paradise, and I had chosen to remain a man. And now, more than ever before, I knew I had to find my way home. I had to warn them. The temptation was too great; the force, once begun, may not be stoppable.

My path to the fissure took me across a meadow of the glass-like grass, which chimed softly with each step I took. A herd of the white, six-legged creatures I had seen before grazed nearby. As I approached, they did not scatter. They simply lifted their heads in perfect unison, their great, dark eyes fixing upon me not with fear, but with a kind of deep, passive enquiry. There was no leader, no signal given; their movements were as one, a single motion flowing through a dozen bodies. I felt a chill that had nothing to do with the evening air. It was the feeling of being observed not by many, but by one, from many points. I walked through the centre of the herd, and they parted for me with the fluid ease of water parting around a stone, their heads turning to follow my progress. Then, as I passed, they closed ranks behind me and resumed their grazing, again in perfect synchrony. The utter silence of the manoeuvre was the most unsettling part of all.

A gentle, cool breeze, smelling of damp earth and something else, something metallic and ozone-like, issued from its depths. The stream that had fed the pool of my first encounter trickled from the lower lip of the fissure, its water unnaturally clear. I peered into the darkness, but it was absolute. My voice, when I called out a tentative “Hello?”, was swallowed by the void, leaving not even the faintest echo. The silence that answered was heavier and more profound than any I had ever known. It was the silence of a mind deep in thought.

For a long time I hesitated. The old, instinctive fears of the dark and the unknown were potent. But a greater fear now gripped me: the fear of being assimilated by this immense, quiet being. What if to enter was to be absorbed? What if the price of knowledge was my own self? I pictured my own consciousness, my memories, my loves and hatreds, my petty vanities and my grand ambitions, all dissolving like a drop of ink in an endless ocean. The prospect was terrifying. And yet, what was the alternative? To live as a castaway on this silent shore, forever a stranger, an anomaly, until my time ran out? No, I could not. I was a man of an age of discovery; to turn back from such a profound mystery was a betrayal of my very nature.

Taking a deep breath, I rummaged in my pockets for the box of matches I still carried; a small, pathetic remnant of my own world’s technology. I struck one. Its tiny flare of chemical fire seemed an act of incredible violence in this tranquil world. Holding it aloft, I stepped across the threshold.

The interior was not a simple cave. The walls were smooth, almost polished, and swirled with faint, pearlescent colours, like the inside of a seashell. They were not rock, or not any rock I knew; they felt faintly yielding and warm to the touch, like living tissue. The floor sloped downwards at a gentle angle, and I followed it, the small circle of my match’s light bobbing before me. The air grew cooler, and the metallic tang stronger. And then I began to notice something else: a low, resonant hum, a sound so deep that I felt it in the bones of my chest more than I heard it with my ears. It was the hum of immense, sleeping power.

My first match burned my fingers and I dropped it, plunging me into a darkness so total it felt like a physical pressure against my eyes. I fumbled for another, my heart hammering. For that brief, blind second, I felt a presence around me, a vast and patient awareness. It was not hostile; it was simply… there. The feeling vanished as my second match flared to life. I saw that the passage had begun to widen, and strange structures were becoming visible in the gloom.

Growing from the walls and floor were crystalline formations, similar to the flora outside, but here they were far more complex and intricate. They formed great, branching, tree-like structures, and through their translucent limbs I could see pulses of soft, blue-white light travelling in complex, rhythmic patterns. They were like the neurons of a stupendous brain, firing in patterns of unimaginable complexity. The hum I felt seemed to emanate from them, a symphony of pure, silent thought. I was not in a cave; I was in a ganglion. I was walking through the physical mind of the world.

I used my matches sparingly, letting my eyes adjust between each one. In the lingering after-images, I saw that the light-pulses within the crystals would change as I drew near, quickening, forming new pathways, as if my presence was a novel stimulus that the mind was actively processing. It was studying me. I felt a wave of intellectual vertigo. How could my small, ape-descended brain even begin to comprehend a consciousness whose thoughts were written in light and crystal across kilometres of living rock?

The downward slope steepened, and the passage opened into a vast chamber. I stood upon a ledge, and before me was a sight that brought me to my knees. The chamber was a sphere of utterly impossible size, and it was filled, from floor to ceiling, with the crystalline network. But here, it all converged. Trillions of light-filaments, each carrying a pulse of that cool, blue light, flowed from every direction into a central point. There, they did not meet, but fed into a globe of pure, incandescent energy, a miniature sun of pure consciousness that hovered in the exact centre of the vast space, motionless and silent, yet vibrating with a power that dwarfed a thunderstorm. The hum was deafening here, a physical force that vibrated every molecule of my body. I had found it. The nexus. The core of the planetary mind.

I had no more matches. I did not need them. The light from the central globe filled the cavern with a soft, analytical blue twilight. I saw that the ledge I was on was one of many, and that other passages, other nerve-ways, converged here from all over the planet. I was in the world’s thalamus, its grand central station of thought and being.

And then, it spoke to me.

There were no words, no sounds. It was a pressure inside my own skull, a flood of pure comprehension that bypassed my senses entirely. It was a sensation of being known, utterly and completely, in an instant. It sifted through my memories, my knowledge, my emotions, not as a thief, but as a librarian cataloguing a new book. I felt the grief of my departures, the thrill of my discoveries, the deep, abiding loneliness of my journey. I felt it understand the concepts of war, of disease, of envy, of my chaotic, self-destructive, beautiful world.

There was a sense of profound, ancient sadness in its response. A sorrow for the pain of individuality.

And then it made its offer.

Again, there were no words, only a feeling, an invitation. It showed me what it was. It was the final destination of life, the escape from the brutal calculus of evolution. It had begun, aeons ago, as all life does, in struggle. But some organisms had learned cooperation, then symbiosis, then merger. The individual became the colony, the colony became the biome, the biome became the world. It had been a slow, inexorable process of unification, a surrendering of the painful, isolated ‘I’ for the serene, eternal ‘We’.

It offered me this peace. It offered an end to striving, an end to fear, an end to my crushing solitude. It could take my mind, my little flicker of awareness, and weave it into its own grand tapestry. I would not die. I would become a part of something immortal, something perfect. My griefs would be soothed, my anxieties erased. I would be one with the tranquil deer, the silent trees, the mind of the planet itself. I would know peace.

The offer was a siren song of almost irresistible power. My will, which I had always considered my strongest asset, felt like a flimsy dam against an ocean. I felt my sense of self begin to fray at the edges. My name, my past, the face of my beloved Weena from that other, aborted future, it all began to seem distant, unimportant. Why cling to this small, painful shard of identity when I could be part of the whole? The temptation was an ecstasy, a promise of a final, blissful homecoming.

I took a step towards the edge of the ledge, my eyes fixed on the glowing heart of the world-mind. One more step and I would cast myself down, into that light, into that peace. My end. My apotheosis.

But then, a memory, unbidden, surfaced from the depths of the mind it was trying to erase. It was a small thing. I was a child in my father’s workshop, and I had built a clumsy little boat of wood and string. I had launched it in a puddle, and it had promptly capsized. I had cried in frustration, and my father had laughed, and then he had shown me how to balance the mast. It was a memory of failure, of imperfection, of learning. It was a memory of two separate minds, a father and a son, connecting through a shared, clumsy act of creation. It was a memory of love, born not of fusion, but of difference.

That tiny, imperfect memory was my anchor.

It was everything this world-mind was not. It was chaos, it was failure, it was struggle, and it was the seed of something new. In that moment, I understood the true horror of the mind’s offer. It was not offering life; it was offering an end to it. The peace it promised was the peace of utter stasis. There was no art here, no science, no laughter, no tears, no love between two separate beings. There was only the endless, silent, self-contemplation of a single, lonely god.

The spell broke.

With a cry that was torn from my very soul, I recoiled from the edge. The pressure in my head intensified, no longer a gentle invitation but a powerful, commanding force. *Stay. Join. Be at peace.*

But I was a man. And a man’s nature is to struggle.

“No!” I screamed, and the sound of my own voice, raw and individual and defiant, was a weapon. I turned and ran, scrambling back into the passage from which I came. The hum behind me rose in pitch, and I felt a wave of profound, cosmic disappointment wash over me, the sorrow of a god whose prayer has been rejected. It was a feeling more terrible than any anger.

I ran blindly in the dark, stumbling, falling, scraping my hands and knees on the living walls. I could feel it trying to reclaim me, trying to soothe my panic, trying to pull me back into its serene embrace. I fought it with every fibre of my being, clinging to the images of my own chaotic world: a crowded train, a shouting politician, a crying baby, a painter’s frustrated stroke. I clung to the glorious, beautiful imperfection of it all.

Finally, I saw a pale rectangle of light ahead. The entrance. I burst out of the fissure and collapsed onto the chiming grass, gasping the free air into my lungs. The sun had set, and the sky was filled with a multitude of unfamiliar stars. I lay there, shaking, a single, dissonant note in a world of perfect harmony. I had seen the future, and I had refused it. I had been offered paradise, and I had chosen to remain a man. And now, more than ever before, I knew I had to find my way home. I had to warn them. The temptation was too great; the force, once begun, may not be stoppable.

I peered into the vast, red-lit gloom. The chamber was filled with machinery, great, dark shapes of metal whose purpose I could not guess. There were spinning flywheels, and gliding levers, and the slow, inexorable crawl of conveyor belts carrying dark lumps of something into the deeper shadows. And among this machinery, I saw them. The Morlocks. They were everywhere. Scores of them, perhaps hundreds. They were just as the one I had seen above: dull white, with the same large, sensitive, greyish-red eyes. They were naked, save for the matted, flaxen hair that grew on their heads and backs. Some were tending the machines, their small, deft hands moving with a practiced speed. Others were clambering over the gantries and frameworks, their movements strangely spider-like. They seemed to pay me no mind, though I was now standing in the full glow from the shaft opening. I realised that their large eyes, so sensitive to the brilliant sunlight of the Upper World, were likely blinded by the direct, if feeble, light of a match; but this diffuse, red light was their natural element.

For a long time I simply watched, my mind struggling to process the scene. This was the industry that supported the idyllic life of the Eloi. This was the price of their perfect, effortless society. It was a vision of Hell, but a Hell of labour, not of punishment. These creatures were not demons; they were workers. They moved with a listless, mechanical efficiency, their faces devoid of any expression I could read. There was no joy, no anger, no hope. There was only the endless, rhythmic task. As my eyes adapted to the gloom, I began to see more details. I saw that they were eating. In a corner of the great cavern, a group of them were gathered around a low, stone table. A conveyor belt brought something to them from a darker part of the cavern, and they would take it and eat it. I could not see what it was, but a new and more terrible thought began to form in my mind. The Eloi were strict frugivores. The land was rich with fruit. What, then, did the Morlocks eat? Down here, in the barren heart of the earth, there were no fruits, no vegetables. The thought was so appalling that I refused to entertain it. I told myself that they must cultivate vast fungal gardens in some deeper cavern, or perhaps synthesise their food. And yet, the suspicion lingered, a cold and venomous thing in the back of my mind.

I was startled from my observations by a sudden change in the chamber. The great piston slowed its rhythm, and a hush fell over the clattering machinery. The Morlocks stopped their work, their pale heads turning as one towards a particular direction. I followed their gaze. From a large tunnel leading out of the far side of the chamber, a new sound was approaching. It was the wail of a siren, a mournful, rising and falling note that echoed through the vast space. It was, I realised, a dinner bell. The Morlocks on the factory floor began to move, not with the languid pace of their work, but with a new and disturbing eagerness. They scurried towards the low stone table, their white bodies a writhing mass in the red light. I felt a surge of revulsion. They were no longer listless mechanics; they were hungry animals. And then I saw what was on the table. A new conveyor had brought their meal. It was not fungus. It was not some synthetic nutrient paste. The object on the table was small, and clad in a tunic of the same bright fabric the Eloi wore. It was still. I felt the blood drain from my face. My heart hammered against my ribs, a frantic counterpoint to the slowing piston.

The appalling truth, the final, ghastly secret of this world, crashed down upon me. I had seen the Eloi's fear of the dark. I had wondered at their lack of graves. I had puzzled over the relationship between these two species. Now I understood. The Eloi were not the masters of the Morlocks. They were their cattle. For countless generations, the Morlocks had toiled for their masters above. They had woven their clothes, prepared their food, and maintained their Eden. But the relationship had changed. Perhaps food had grown scarce in the Underworld. Perhaps some ancient resentment had finally boiled over. The Morlocks, with their machinery and their brute strength, had turned the tables. But they had not simply overthrown the Eloi. Their relationship was now a grotesque symbiosis. The Morlocks still tended to the Eloi, still provided for their gentle, useless lives. They were their shepherds. And, from time to time, they came up in the darkness to cull their flock.

I looked at the beautiful, indolent people of the Upper World in a new light. They were not simply decadent; they were doomed. They were children raised in a beautiful, sunlit nursery, unaware that they were being fattened for the slaughter. Their lives of ease and beauty were a sham, a fleeting dream before the inevitable, dark awakening. And I, in my foolishness, had been living among them, unarmed and unwary, a larger, more curious specimen of livestock. The thought made my skin crawl. That soft thing I had touched in the ruins, the creature that had fled from me, had it been hunting? Was that its purpose in the Upper World? The instinctive dread of wild beasts I had felt was not an ancient, irrational fear. It was a perfectly rational premonition of the truth.

A wave of nausea and terror swept over me. I had to escape. I had to get back to the surface, back to the daylight, back to the fragile safety of the Time Machine. I began to climb, my hands shaking, my mind a vortex of horror. I did not dare look down again. I did not want to see the culmination of that dreadful feast. I climbed with the desperate strength of pure fear, the sounds of the Underworld fading below me. The rhythmic throb of the piston, the clatter of machinery, the eager scrabbling of the Morlocks; it all merged into a single, nightmarish symphony. I did not stop until my head broke into the clean, fresh air of the surface, and I saw the blessed circle of blue sky above. I scrambled out of the well, gasping, and lay trembling on the turf, like a man who has just escaped from his own grave. The sun was warm on my face, and the air was filled with the scent of flowers and the gentle laughter of the Eloi. But it was no longer a paradise to me. It was a butcher’s garden. Every beautiful flower, every graceful palace, was tainted by the charnel house below. I looked at the carefree Eloi flitting past, and I saw not innocent children, but ghosts, dancing towards their doom. And I knew that I could not stay here. My investigation was complete. The answer to the riddle of this world was more terrible than any I could have imagined. I had to find my Time Machine. And I had to find Weena. I could not leave her here. I could not leave her to the dark.
